subject: Cognitive Science
title: First Principles Thinking
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: First Principles Thinking.

hook.text: Everyone said batteries cost $600 per kWh. Elon Musk asked what the raw materials cost. Answer: $80.

buildup.text: First principles thinking strips away assumptions and reduces a problem to its fundamental truths.

discovery.text: Aristotle defined it: a first principle is the most basic truth that cannot be deduced from anything else.

twist.text: It's cognitively expensive. Most daily decisions should use analogy. Reserve first principles for big bets.

climax.text: When everyone is reasoning by analogy, first principles thinkers see possibilities others can't.

punchline.text: Break it down to what's actually true.

quiz.question: What is first principles thinking?
options: Breaking problems down to fundamental truths

details.summary: First principles thinking breaks problems down to their most fundamental truths rather than reasoning by analogy. Instead of copying what others do, you identify the core constraints and build solutions from scratch. Elon Musk famously used this approach to reduce rocket costs.
details.whyItMatters: Reasoning by analogy keeps you trapped in conventional solutions. First principles thinking unlocks innovation by questioning every assumption.
takeaways: Break problems down to their most basic verified truths
Question assumptions rather than copying existing solutions
First principles enable novel solutions to old problems

faq.question: What is the difference between first principles and analogy?
faq.answer: Analogy says: others do it this way, so I should too. First principles asks: what do I know to be fundamentally true, and what can I build from there? Analogy is faster but limits you to incremental improvements. First principles is slower but can produce breakthroughs.

faq.question: When should you use first principles thinking?
faq.answer: Use it when conventional approaches have failed, when a field seems stuck, or when costs seem unreasonably high. It is too slow for every decision. Reserve it for important problems where existing solutions feel inadequate or where innovation could create significant value.
